claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by the degree of local chemical ordering.
The combination of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness is governed by local chemical ordering.
Strong Al–transition-metal interactions, particularly Al–Ni and Al–Co interactions, promote B2-like ordering.
Enhanced short-range order lowers the free energy of the ordered phase relative to the disordered matrix.
The nominal starting alloy has incipient B2-type clusters in a largely disordered BCC or FCC matrix.
Fast quenching minimizes chemical ordering relative to slow cooling followed by aging.
Slow cooling followed by aging at 700°C for 24 hours enhances short-range chemical order and B2-like cluster formation.
Chemical ordering produces nanoscale heterogeneities that obstruct dislocation motion at high temperature.
Ordered nanoscale heterogeneities provide sites for irradiation-defect recombination.
Chemical ordering tailors crack-propagation pathways at cryogenic temperatures.
Increasing short-range chemical order will enhance retention of the ordered phase relative to the fast-quenched baseline.
Increasing short-range chemical order will improve high-temperature strength relative to the fast-quenched baseline.
Increasing short-range chemical order will increase radiation tolerance, as indicated by lower radiation-induced defect density.
Increasing short-range chemical order will maintain or improve cryogenic toughness relative to the fast-quenched baseline.
A moderate increase in short-range chemical order is beneficial, whereas excessive ordering may cause brittleness.
The proposed relationship applies near compositions where ordered and disordered phases coexist.
The proposed relationship may not apply after complete ordering or formation of substantially different phase constituents such as coarse precipitates.

contradictions.description: The prediction permits cryogenic toughness merely to be maintained, but the falsification rule can treat the absence of significant improvement in cryogenic toughness as falsifying.

Formation of unexpected phases is described as outside the hypothesis's applicability boundary, yet it is also listed as an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis rather than establish that the experiment left its stated domain.
